full_judgment:
Md. Muzammel Hossain CJ. This Criminal Appeal No.35 of 2010 by leave and the Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal No.304 of 2007 are directed against the impugned judgment and order dated 04-04-2007 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division discharging the Rules in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.11080 of 2006 and Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.9954 of 2006 (Wherein the leave petitioners in Criminal Petition No.304 of 2007 appeared as Advocates for the accused petitioners) refusing to quash the proceedings in Fatullah P.S. Case No. 125 dated 27.04.2006 under sections 406/420/506 of the Penal Code pending in the Court of Magistrate. 1st Class, Narayangonj (South) and making some remarks and observations against the Advocate -Petitioners who seek to have such remarks and observations expunged.

2. The relevant facts of the case for disposal of the Criminal Appeal are that Md. Habib Jamal, the appellant filed Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.11080 of 2006 and two other accused persons, namely, A.K.M. Iftekhar Ahmed and A.K.M. Mustafizur Rahman as petitioners filed the aforesaid Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.9954 of 2006 for quashing the proceedings of Fatullah P.S. Case No.125 dated 27.04.2006 under sections 406/420/506 of the Penal Code pending in the Court of Magistrate, 1st Class, Narayangonj (South). The facts of the Fatullah P.S. Case No.125 dated 27-04-2006, in brief, are that on 24-04-2006 one Shimul Barua, a Director of two Knitwear Companies (EEC Bangla Knitwears Ltd. and Tanmoy and Tonny Knitwears Ltd) filed a petition of complaint in the Court of Magistrate, First Class, Narayangonj (South) against Md. Habib Jamal (the appellant), the Company Secretary, A.K.M. Iftekhar Ahmed, the Managing Director, A.K.M. Mustafizur Rahman, the Senior Vice-Present and Mizanur Rahman, the Branch Manager of the Eastern Insurance Company Ltd.

<u>3. The allegations was that the complainant took two fire insurance policies dated 27.10.2005 and 29.12.2005 from the Eastern Insurance Company Ltd. for a total of Tk. 5 crores to cover their two factories. A fire broke out in both the factories on 16.01.2006 at 2.00 a.m. causing extensive damage to the factory and destroying all the goods and raw materials. As a result, the complainant lodged an insurance claim which was repudiated and rejected by the Insurance Company save and except agreeing to pay a sum of Tk. 1 Crore only. The complainant made several representations for receiving the claimed amount but to no avail.</u>

4. The learned Magistrate upon examining the complainant passed an order of 24.04.2006 directing the Officer -in-Charge of Fatullah Police Station to take necessary action in accordance with law. The Officer -in-Charge on 27.04.2006 treated the petition of complaint as the First Information Report (FIR) and started Fatullah P.S. Case No.125 dated 27.04.2006 under sections 406/420/506 of the Penal Code against the appellant, three others, namely, A.K.M. Iftekhar Ahmed, the Managing Director, A.K.M. Mustafizur Rahman, the Senior Vice-Present and Mizanur Rahman, the Branch Manager.

5. In addition to the filing of the above Criminal Case, the information on 30.04.2006 instituted a civil suit in the 5th Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka being Money Suit No.23 of 2006 for realization of the same insurance claim of Tk.5 crores under the Insurance Policy.

6. The appellant along with two other co-accused Iftekhar Ahmed and Mustafizur Rahman then surrendered before the High Court Division through Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.6238 of 2006 and prayed for anticipatory bail, whereupon a Division Bench of the High Court Division by order dated 10.05.2006 issued Rule and granted them anticipatory bail.

7. Police after investigation submitted charge sheet in the case before the learned Magistrate on 02.07.2006 against the accused persons including the appellant being Charge sheet No. 400 dated 29.06.2006 under sections 406/420/506(II) of the Penal Code on receipt of which the learned Magistrate, 1st Class Narayangonj (South) by order dated 02.07.2006 cancelled the bail of the appellant and committed him into custody. However, the appellant was enlarged on bail by a subsequent, order dated 09.07.2006 passed by the learned Magistrate and since then the appellant has been on bail.

Grounds of Criminal Appeal

No. 35 of 2010

<u>8. The aforesaid Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.11080 of 2006 filed by the present appellant was heard analogously with Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.9954 of 2006 by a Division Bench of the High Court Division, who by the impugned judgment and Order dated 04.04.2007 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.11080 of 2006 the petitioner -Appellant the instant appeal by leave of this Division, being Criminal Appeal No.35 of 2010, which has arisen out of Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal No.314 of 2007 before this Division. This Division having considered the submissions of the Learned Senior Advocate for the petitioner -appellant granted leave by order dated 25.03.2010 to consider the following grounds:-</u>

<u>1. That the petitioner having rightly invoked the jurisdiction under section 561A of the Code of the Criminal Procedure after submission of Charge Sheet in the case, the High Court Division erred in law I holding by and large that the accused petitioner was not entitled to invoke the jurisdiction under Section 561A without waiting for framing of charge or invoking the provisions of Section 241 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for discharge.</u>

<u>2. That the High Court Division erred in law ad upon fact in discharging the Rule on a wrong technical ground and as such, ought to have quashed the proceeding in question to prevent abuse of the process of the Court upon holding that even if the FIR and Charge Sheet version of the case is taken to be true, the FIR or petition of complaint do not disclose any offence punishable under Sections 406/420/506 of the Penal Code.</u>

<u>3. That the High Court Division ought to have held that even if the allegation in the FIR ad the Charge Sheet, taken as a whole, are to be true, they at best disclose a claim for insurance money against a public limited insurance company and as such, the claim being a civil claim for debt, the said criminal proceeding should not be allowed to continue as a contrivance to put pressure upon the company or its executives for realization of the said civil debt.</u>

Submission in Criminal Appeal

No.35 of 2010

9. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant submits that the appellant having rightly invoked the jurisdiction under Section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure after submission of Charge Sheet in the case, the High Court Division erred in law in holding by and large that the accused appellant was not entitled to invoke the jurisdiction under Section 561A without waiting for framing of charge or invoking the provisions of Section 241A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for discharge. The learned Senior Advocate submits that the High Court Division was in error in not appreciating that even if the allegations in the FIR and the Charge Sheet taken as a whole are to be true, they at best disclose a claim for insurance money against a public limited insurance company and the claim thusbeing a civil claim for debt and the liability, if any, being a civil liability, lodging of criminal case and continuation of criminal proceeding as a device or contrivance to put pressure for realisation of any debt or civil claim being a gross abuse ad misuse of the process of criminal justice system, the proceeding in question is liable to be quashed to let the parties to resolve their civil disputes in a civil court.

10. Mr. Islam then submits that the High Court Division committed an error of law in not holding that the instant criminal proceeding is an abuse of the process of the Court and for the ends of justice the proceeding should be quashed. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Senior Advocate for the appellant finally submits that the High Court Division totally ignored a material fact that the informant having already filed money suit for realization of the said insurance claim, the whole dispute became the subject matter of the said civil suit and as such the High Court Division ought to have held that continuation of any criminal proceeding against the appellant or the self same dispute is utter abuse of the process of the criminal court and as such is liable to be struck down.

11. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, the learned Attorney General, submits that the allegations in the FIR and the Charge Sheet disclose offences punishable under section 406/420/506 of the Penal Code and as such there is no illegality in the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division which does not require any interference by this Division and as such the appeal is liable to be dismissed.

Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal

No. 304 of 2007.

12. This leave petition arises as a result of remarks and observations against the Petitioners who appeared as Advocates in the Criminal Miscellaneous Cases Which are contained in the impugned judgment and order date 04-04-2007 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division. The facts for the disposal of the leave petition are that three of the accused persons, namely, A.K. M. Iftekhar Ahmed, the Managing Director, Md Habib Jamal, Company Secretary and Mr. A. K. M. Mustafizur Rahman, Senior Vice President, of Eastern Insurance company Ltd filed an application in the High Court Division for anticipatory bail, being Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.6238 of 2006 whereupon a Division Bench comprising Mr. Justice Mohammad Abdur Rashid and Mr. Justice Md. Mizanur Rahman Bhuiyan by an order dated 10.05.2006 enlarged them on anticipatory bail till disposal of the Rule or filing of the police report after investigation, whichever is earlier.

13. A copy of the order date 10.05.2006 of High Court Division was received by the Additional District Magistrate, Narayangonj on 24.05.2006, who granted the three accused bail on furnishing of bail bond of Tk.40,000/-each in compliance with the High Court Division's order. The records of the bail and the bail bond were then sent to the Court of Magistrate 1st Class, Narayangonj, who received the same on 31.05.2006 in presence of all three accused fixing 02.07.2006 as the next date of the case.

14. On 02.07.2006, the Magistrate officially received the order of anticipatory bail passed in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.6238 of 2006. On the same day, the Charge Sheet being No. 400 dated 29.06.2006 was also submitted before the Magistrate. On this day, the accused, Habib Jamal, the Company Secretary, was present before the Magistrate upon filing hazira. Since the other two accused, namely, A. K. M. Iftekhar Ahmed and A. K. M. Mustafizur Rahman were not able to reach Narayangonj from Dhaka on time, applications for adjournment were filed on their behalf by their lawyer. It may be mentioned here that there was an "oborodh"(siege) programme observed by the then opposition political parties in Dhaka protesting Government actions. The learned Magistrate holding that because of the anticipatory bail granted till submission of Charge Sheet, the accused were not on bail anymore rejected the adjournment petitions and issued warrants of arrest against them. As regards Habib Jamal, the Company Secretary who was preset before the Court of Magistrate, he was taken into custody and set to jail as there was no application on his behalf. It may be mentioned here that there was a fourth accused named Mizanur Rahman, who was absent on bail on that day, and his bail also cancelled and warrant of arrest was issued against him.

15. In the premises, the accused A.K.M. Iftekhar Ahmed and A.K.M. Mustafizur Rahman filed an application before the High Court Division in the said Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.6238 of 2006 praying for them to be allowed to continue on the same bail as was granted earlier by the High Court Division narrating the facts and circumstances leading to the issuance of warrants of arrest against them followed by consecutive police raids in their houses soon thereafter to arrest them and further expressing apprehension that if they had appeared before the Court of Magistrate in Narayangonj, they would have been refused bail and taken into custody as some of the sitting Ministers of the time were interfering in the proceeding before the Magistrate from behind the scene. The affidavit of this application was affirmed on 10.07.2006 and the application was listed as item No. 16 on 11.07.2006 in the Daily Cause List of the Division Bench presided over by Mr. Justice Mohammed Abdur Rashid. In the application, at paragraph Nos.5, 6, 7 and 8 the entire matter starting from granting of anticipatory bail up to issuance of warrants of arrest on 02.07.2006 as well as circumstances leading to filing of Charge Sheet was elaborately mentioned in details and there was no concealment of any fact whatsoever that there were warrants of arrest against these two accused Iftekhar Ahmed ad Mustafizur Rahman Certified copy of the order sheet of the Court of Magistrate was annexed to the said application as Annexure "B-1" Simultaneously, the aforesaid two accused, namely A. K. M. Iftekhar Ahmed and A.K.M Mustafizur Rahman, also filed an application under Section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 being Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 9954 of 2006 for quashment of the said Fatullah P.S. Case No. 125 dated 27.04.2004 in which, as a measure of abundant caution, a prayer for ad-interim bail was inserted in the prayer portion of the petition by hand, which was initiated by the Affidavit Commissioner, such prayer was added in case the earlier mentioned petition for allowing them to continue on the same bail was not entertained by the High Court Division. The affidavit in this petition was also affirmed on 10.07.2006. This Petition was listed as "In Re" item No. 170 on 11.07.2006 in Daily Cause List of the Division Bench presided over by Mr. Justice Mohammed Abdur Rashid. It may be noted here that in the quashment petition, at paragraph Nos. 7, 8, 9 and 10 the entire matter starting from granting of anticipatory bail upto issuance of warrants of arrest on 02.07.2006 was elaborated mentioned in details and there was no concealment of any fact whatsoever that there was warrants of arrest against these two accused. The order sheet of the Court of Magistrate was not annexed here as the same was already annexed as Annexure-"B -1" to the other application in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.6238 of 2006.

16. On the prayer of the :Learned Advocates for the petitioners, both the aforesaid listed items (i.e. item Nos. 16 and 170 of the Daily Cause List of 11.07.2006) were taken up on 11.07.2006 but were listed for the next day as item Nos. 13 and 19 respectively in the Daily Cause List of 12,07.2006. On 12.07.2006 the application in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.6238 of 2006 ad the quashment petition under 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure were taken up for hearing together and the learned Judges after hearing the entire facts and circumstances in the matter issued the Rule in the petition under Section 561 A the Code of Criminal Procedure, stayed all further proceedings of the criminal case and also granted ad-interim bail, which was registered as Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.9954 of 2006, and rejected the other application in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.6238 of 2006 being not pressed.

17. On 26.07.2006, the information filed a application for being added as a party in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.9954 of 2006 and a Division Bench of the High Court Division by an order of the same date ordered the application to be kept on record as the Stage was to look after the interest of the informant; however, the Learned Advocate for the informant was permitted to assist the State. It may be noted here that in the application of the informant there was no allegation of suppression of facts or the accused were fugitive.

18. In the meantime, the third accused Habib Jamal, the Company Secretary, who was earlier taken into custody on 02.07.2006 by the Magistrate, upon being released on bail filed Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 11080 of 2006 for quashment of the Fatullah P.S. Case No, 125 dated 27.04.2009 whereupon the Rule was issued and stay was granted on 31.07.2006 by the Division Bench presided over by Mr. Justice Abdur Rashid.

19. The informant filed a counter-Affidavit dated 14.03.2007 in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.9954 of 2006 and a Supplementary Affidavit dated 28.03.2007 stating amongst others that there being warrants of arrest issued by the Magistrate against the accused, they were fugitives and not entitled to any relief in the case and that the remedy for the accused was to file an application under Section 241A of the Code. The informant ignored the fact that the High Court Division itself granted the accused anticipatory bail while issuing the Rule in the quashment petition. The informant never alleged in the Counter Affidavit that there was any suppression or concealment of fact by the accused before the Court while controverting the statement in the petition para wise.

20. The aforesaid Criminal Miscellaneous Case Nos.9954 of 2006 and 11080 of 2006 were heard analogously be a Division Bench comprising Mr. Justice Sharif Uddin Chaklader and Mr. Justice Sheikh Abdul Awal, who by the impugned judgment and order dated 04.04.2007 discharged the Rule and made the aforementioned adverse remarks and observations which are being sought to be expunged in the interest of justice and fairness. It may be noted here that according to the judgment itself, the matter was heard only on 04.03.2007, the accused were represented by the learned Advocate, Mr. Sheikh Hassan Arif (the petitioner No.2) in Criminal Petition for to Appeal No.304 of 2007, who prayed for an adjournment on account of the preoccupation of Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Senior Advocate (the petitioner No.1) on that day in another Court. However, the High Court Division kept the matter as "part heard" in keeping with the practice developed by the said Division Bench, although in actual fact no hearing took place. On 19.03.2007, the learned Senior Advocate appeared and concluded his submissions on that day and the matter was fixed for judgment on 21.03.2007, which is also evident from the order sheet of the case. On 19.03.2007, when the hearing concluded, there was no allegation of any suppression or concealment of fact from any quarter nor was there any allegation of the accused being fugitives. Iv view of the Statements made in paragraph Nos. 7, 8, 9 and 10 of the Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.9954 of 2006, which were perused by the learned Judges and referred to by the learned Advocates for the petitioners, the allegations of concealment or suppression of facts or misleading the Court or practicing any alleged fraud on the Court did not arise at all, nor did any question arise as to the accused being fugitives. There was a full disclosure of all facts including the warrants of arrest.

21. On the day fixed for the judgment, i.e. on 21.03.2007, the High Court Division on its own motion adjourned the delivery of the judgment for one week. Thereafter, on 28.03.2007 the learned Judges also adjourned the delivery of judgment on its own motion to 03.04.2007. Then on 03.04.2007, the learned Judges of the High Court Division again adjourned on its own motion the delivery of judgment to the next day, i.e. 04.04.2007, when the Rule was discharged by judgment in a separate sheet. It appears from the nothing in the order sheet that on 21.03.2007, learned Advocate for the accused and the learned Advocate for the informant were present in the Court and from the note sheet of 28.03.2007 it also appears that the learned Senior Advocate for the accused and that the learned Advocate for the informant were present in the Court. It further appears from the nothing in the order Sheet that on 03.04.2007 no lawyer from any side was present.

22. The petitioners have refinined from specifically quoting in the petition the remarks ad observations sought to be expunged in order to avoid repetition of defamatory, objectionable, virulent and abusive language except when it is totally unavoidable, but craved leave of this Court of refer to the same at the time of hearing and point it out from the judgment itself.

23. The learned Judges after very briefly narrating the fact of the allegations in the complaint took up the question of the accused being fugitive from justice before entering into the merit of the case. It appears from the judgment that the learned Judges considered the petition under Section 561A of the Code which means that the learned Judges of the Division Bench read and considered paragraph Nos. 7, 8, 9 and 10 of the petition in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 9954 of 2006 . Therefore, it was to their knowledge that the accused fully disclosed to the Court not only the fact that on 02.07.2006 the Magistrate issued warrants of arrest against them, but also the fact and circumstances for which they could not be present in the Court, of Magistrate for which their lawyer had to file a time petition on their behalf, as well as the fact that another accused Habib Jamal, who was personally present was taken into custody by the Magistrate being biased. In paragraph No. 8 of the petition, there was a description of facts as to how the Charge Sheet dated 29.06.2006 came to be sub-mitted on 02.07.2006 so as to take the accused in custody when they were present in Court.

24. It is stated that the High Court Division was wrong to observe that "it appears from the order sheets annexed with the affidavit that despite granting several adjournments on the prayer of the learned Advocates for the accused petitioners for filing counter -affidavit to controvert the allegation of being fugitive, they did not file any counter affidavit" inasmuch that there was no prayer on the part of the petitioners for adjournment for filing counter-affidavit. There was no allegation against the Advocate petitioners as lawyers form the informant's side and therefore there was no question of any counter affidavit by them. Insofar as informant's counter-affidavit is concerned, the informant described the accused as "fugitive from justice" as there were warrants arrest issued by the Magistrate on 02.07.2006. The accused themselves in their petition fully disclosed this fact as well as the order. In the premises, the High Court Division's finding that "accused -petitioners without appearing or surrendering before the learned Magistrate, appeared before this Court upon concealing the fact that their bail was cancelled and the there was an order of warrants of arrest issued against them and made the aforesaid illegal prater for bail." Is totally contrary to the records an averments of the accused in their quashment petition. Besides, there is by implication an accusation against the Advocate petitioners in this regard. The Advocate petitioners never sought any adjournment for filing any Counter-Affidavit to controvert the allegations of being fugitive. There was no such allegation Secondly, the question of seeking any adjournment after the conclusion of the hearing does not arise.

<u>25. It is state that the High Court Division upon making the aforesaid wrongful observation as quoted hereinabove proceeded to wrongly and unfairly observe that "It is very unfortunate that the learned advocate for the accused petitioners moved this Court and obtained rule, order of stay and bail by suppressing the fact that the bail of the accused petitioners was canceled and there was an order of warrant of arrest hanging against the accused petitioners" Inasmuch as paragraph No. 9 of the quashment petition expressly and specifically discloses the order dated 02.07.2006 of the Magistrate and issuance of the warrants of arrest against the accused.</u>

26. It is also stated that the High Court Division made some unkind and harsh remarks about the Advocate petitioners and their conduct by referring to insertion by hand in the prayer to the effect" enlarge the petitioners on ad-interim bail" and observing that it was neither initiated by the affidavit Commissioner nor corrected with the leave of the court and the initials against the insertion does not tally with the other initials of the Affidavit Commissioner inasmuch as the initial of the Affidavit Commissioner here was exactly the same as his initial made next to the date of the Affidavit as made at page 16 of the quashment petition.

27. It is stated that the High Court Division very harshly and without any supporting evidence and acting contrary to the disclosure of the petition observed that the aforesaid insertion was made to mislead the Court to obtain favourable order and it was done upon practicing fraud on the Court for degrading the position of the Court. At this state of the Judgment, the learned Judges went to the extent of being abusive about the Advocate petitioners and went to the extent of calling names when they observed that "the accused persons being in high position, both in money and status, taking advantage of the trust of the Court on "high sounding Advocates" showed thumb to the process of law and Court"

28. It is further stated that the High Court Division was to observe and implicate the Advocate petitioners while observing that "by practicing fraud upon the Court, the Court has been misled ad the Rule was obtained on 12.07.2006 from this Court. From the facts and circumstances aforesaid it is clear that this fact (i.e. cancellation of bail as and issuance of warrant of arrest) was known both to the learned Advocate as well as the accused -petitioners )" inasmuch as the aforesaid fact was not concealed at all but was fully ad entirely disclosed and in that view of the matter, the High Court Division's finding in this respect was wrong and incorrect.

29. It is also stated that the finding of the High Court Division at a later stage of the judgment to the effect that "this is called a fraud practiced upon the Court. Had this fact been known to the Rule issuing Court, then the Court probably would not issue the Rule, From the Rule issuing order we find that the learned Judges enlarged the accused petitioners on ad-interim bail subject to the satisfaction of the Deputy commissioner, Narayangonj. It is very painstaking that a senior lawyer of such stature, to whom the Court always places trust, if takes the advantage in such manner without respecting the Canons of professional Conduct and Etiquette as provided for in the Bar Council Order and Rules, 1972, then the question may arise as to what the junior lawyers will learn and practice", was wrong inasmuch as it fixes the blame on the Advocate -petitioners as well as questioned their professional conduct and etiquette, which was not only not necessary for disposal of the Rule but also factually incorrect and wrong. Furthermore, such finding relating to the professional conduct of the advocates ought not to have been given without first giving the Advocates an opportunity of being heard by informing them of the allegation the learned Judges held against them. Besides, such finding as well as other observations and remarks freely and frequently resorted to by the learned Judges against the Advocate petitioners in the Judgment create an impression of bias of the learned Judges against them, particularly the Advocate petitioner no.1, in the minds of any reasonable reader of the Judgment.

30. It is stated that the learned Judges were not content to leave the matter at rest there after making such unwarranted, uncalled for unsubstantiated, unjust and extraneous observations as referred to herein above; that their Lordships after concluding the judgment, discharging the Rule an ordering for sending the down lower court records and communication for the order at once, proceeded to add another eleven pages entirely on the Advocate petitioners starting with the words "Now on the conduct of the learned Advocate   This part of the judgment demonstrates the bias of the learned Judges against the Advocate Petitioners. Such observations and findings are clear violations of the principles of natural justice. These observations were unjust and unkind to say the least. They are completely extraneous to the subject matter of the Rule. Many decisions have been cited here, all of which are inappropriate to the facts and circumstances and the same have been referred to out of context.

31. It is stated that the second part of the judgment unnecessarily and harshly dealt with the Advocate -Petitioners, which was not at all necessary and called for Furthermore, these observations were made after discharging the Rules on merit ad appeared to be totally extraneous to the merit of the case. Such observations as have been made touching upon integrity and conduct of the Advocate Petitioners as professional lawyers ought not to have without giving them an opportunity of being heard.

32. The Advocate -Petitioners were shocked to read the impugned remarks and observations when the certified copy was obtained for the client to prefer Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal in the Appellate Division, even more distressing is the part appearing after disposal of the case by discharging the Rule. The Advocate -Petitioners find it difficult to believe that a Division Bench would be so harsh and unkind as to make such adverse remarks against Advocates practicing in this Court and these adverse remarks and observations were liable to the expunged.

Submission in Criminal Petition for leave to Appeal

No. 304 of 2007.

33. In Criminal Petition for leave to Appeal No.304 of 2007 the Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the Advocate -Petitioners, submits that the High Court Division erred in law and facts in making the impugned remarks and observations against the Advocate - Petitioners inasmuch as such remarks and observations are based upon a wrongful finding that the order of Rule, stay of proceedings and ad-interim bail was obtained by suppressing the fact that warrants of arrest had been issued against the accused, when in reality the fact of the said warrants, including the circumstances leading to their issuance, was expressly narrated in detail in the petition for quashment.

34. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, submits that the impugned remarks and observations against the Advocate -petitioners are liable to be expunged inasmuch as they are based upon finding and premises which are contrary to the records of the case, including the orders and office notes recorded in the order sheet of the case. He also submits that the impugned remarks and observations are extraneous to the merit of the case and were not relevant to the disposal of the rule issued in the petition for quashment, besides being uncalled for, unwarranted, unsubstantiated and unjust.

35. The learned Senior Advocate for the Advocate -petitioners submits that the impugned remarks and observations are liable to be expunged for ends of justice inasmuch as they have been made without giving the petitioner and opportunity of being heard upon being informed of the allegations against them, which casts aspersions upon their professional conduct and etiquette. He then submits that the impugned remarks and observations give an impression of bias of the learned Judges against the Advocate-Petitioner no.1, in the minds of any reasonable person reading the judgment. Mr. Malunudul Islam, the learned Senior Advocate for the Advocate-Petitioners finally submits that the impugned remarks and observations made by the learned Judge, being adverse to the Advocate Petitioners and made after disposal of the case on merit by discharging the Rule, having no bearing on the case before the learned Judges and the same are inapplicable and inappropriate to the facts and circumstances and have been out of context and these adverse remarks and observations are liable to be expunged.

36. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, the learned Attorney General, appearing for the respondents submits that he has no objection if the adverse, unjust and extraneous remarks and observations as referred to above are expunged. He finally submits that a guideline should be given to the learned Judges as to how to deal with the conduct of the learned Advocates who have failed to maintain the dignity, honour and prestige of the court thereby discharging the Cannons of professional Conduct and Etiquette as provided for in the Bangladesh Bar Council Order and Rules 1972.

37. We have heard the learned Advocates and perused the leave granting order and concise statements in Criminal Appeal No.35 of 2010, Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal No.304 of 2007 and the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division and the other materials on record. Discussions and Finding

Criminal Appeal No. 35 of 2010

<u>38. In this case the appellant moved the High Court Division under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashment of the proceedings in Fatulla P.S. Case No. 125 dated 27.04.2009 under sections 406/420/506 of the Panel Code pending in the Court of Magistrate, First Class, Narayangonj. The High Court Division has the jurisdiction to pass an order to secure the ends of justice and therefore for that purpose the High Court Division is competent to entertain an application not provided by the Code. The exercise of inherent power of the High Court Division under section 561A of the Court of is to secure the ends of justice in the facts and circumstances of each case. The inherent Jurisdiction is attracted I three cases, Firstly, "to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Code". Secondly, "to prevent abuse of the process of any Court", Thirdly, "otherwise to secure the ends of justice". In the case of Md. Shahabuddin vs the State 40 DLR (AD) 69 at page 74 para 12 Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed while expressing the majority view of the Court observed that "the High Court Division got inherent power under section 561A Crl. P.C. to make such orders as may be necessary 'to prevent abuse of the process of any court or other wise to secure the ends of the justice. "This power may be exercised only in those cases which are not covered by any specific provisions of the Code. The inherent power of the Court is undefined and indefinite and as such it must be exercised very sparingly and with great and with great caution".</u>

<u>39. Speaking for the Appellate Division Mr. Justice Ruhul Islam in the case of Bangladesh v. Tan Kheng Hgck, reported in 31 DLR (AD) 69 observed as under ; "21 Of course, facts of a particular case may call for interference under section 561A of the Code where even on the admitted facts no criminal case stands against the accused. And further prolongation of the prosecution would amount to harassment to an innocent person, that is, above of the process of the Court. There might also be cases where it appears that there is a legal bar against the institution or continuance of the proceedings the High Court would be justified in quashing under section 561A of the Code. Examples may not provide an inflexible rule which would govern the exercise of the inherent power of the High Court under section 561A of the Code, but the power being extraordinary it ought to be used sparingly, carefully and with utmost caution only where such exercise is justified by the tests laid down in the section itself." In the instant case the complainant lodged and insurance claim which was repudiated by the insurance Company thought they agreed to pay a sum of Taka 1 crore instead of five crores as claimed. From the facts of the case it appears that the informant lodged the claim to the Insurance Company which is a civil liability on the part of the company to pay the same. But instead of agreeing to pay the total amount of Tk. 5 crores the company agreed to pay Tk. 1 crore. It is also the informants case that the made unsuccessfully several representations to the company for realization of the claimed amount but to no avail. There is no allegation that the Insurance Company deceived the informant or denied the very existence of the insurance policy. It appears that in the instant case the Magistrate upon examining the complainant directed the Officer-in-Charge, Fatullah police station to take necessary action in accordance with law, Accordingly, the petition of complaint was treated as an FIR and Fatullah P.S. Case No.125 date 27.04.2006 under sections 061420/506 of the Penal Code was started the appellant and two other Senior Executives of the Company. Police submitted Charge Sheet under sections 406/420/506 of the Penal Code. If the allegations made in the FIR and the Charge Sheet taken at the face value accepted in their entirety are taken to be true, they at best disclose a claim for insurance money against the Insurance Company and they do not constitute the offence alleged. Rather the claim being a civil claim for debt, the criminal proceeding should not be allowed to continue as a contrivance to put pressure upon the company or its executives for realization of the civil debt. In the circumstances, the High Court Division should have quashed the proceeding of the case. In this context it is pertinent to refer to the case of Syed Md. Hashem v. State 48 DLR (AD) 87 wherein this Division held that a criminal proceeding can only be quashed after cognizance has been taken and process issued thereupon subject to the fundamental principle that the power of quashing is and should be very sparingly exercised and only to prevent the abuse of the process of the Court. In the case of Syed Ali Mir v. Omar Ali reported in 42 DLR (AD) 240 there was a money claim which was not the outcome of a particular transaction but arose after year end accounting following regular business between the parties. On settlement of accounts at the end of the stipulated period some money fails due to one party from the other party and the other party fails to pay the dues. This Division further held that the allegation that dues were allowed to accrue dishonestly, neither attract an offence under section 420 not under section 406 nor under any other provisions of law. The whole allegation in the petition of complaint, even it true, cannot form the basis of any criminal proceeding much less for cheating for the alleged liabilities incurred is essentially civil in nature. Accordingly, the appeal was allowed and the proceedings was quashed by the Appellate Division. In the case of MS Khawja v. State 17 DLR (SC) 153 the Supreme Court of Pakistan held that to quash a judicial proceeding in order to "secure the ends of justice" would involve a finding that if permitted to continue, the proceeding would defeat the ends of justice or, in other words, would either operate or perpetuate an injustice. The Supreme Court further held that do find an "abuse", it would be necessary to see in the proceeding, a perversion of the purpose of the law such as to cause harassment to an innocent party, to bring about delay, or where the machinery of justice is engaged in an operation from which no result in furtherance of justice can accrue and similar per-verse results. In the instant case the High Court Division erred in law to hold that accused appellant was not entitled to invoke the jurisdiction under section 561A of the Code without waiting for framing of charge or invoking the provisions of section 241 A of the code for dis-charge because exercise of inherent jurisdiction of the High Court Division under section 561 A of the Code depends on the facts of each case as much as the instant case is a proper case for exercise of such jurisdiction. We may refer to the decision of the case of Abdul Quader Chowdhury vs. State 28 DLR (AD) 38 wherein this Division held that the consensus of judicial opinion is that it is not possible, desirable or expedient of lay down any inflexible rule which should govern the exercise of this inherent jurisdiction. The exercise of this jurisdiction will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on the admitted facts no case can stand against the accused and that a further prolongation of the prosecution would amount of harassment to an innocent party and abuse of the process of the Court. Accordingly to Ruhul Islam, J, "the HCD can exercise its inherent power when it is absolutely necessary for doing justice that is, to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice." This Division in the case of State v. Md. Nasim 57 DLR (AD) 114 held that from the first information report it appears that contents thereof even if accepted in its entirety no prima facie case is disclosed and, as such the High Court Division rightly passed the impugned judgment and order in quashing the proceeding.</u>

<u>40. In view of the foregoing discussions and observations we are of the view that in the instant case the High Court Division should have exercised its jurisdictions under section 561A of the Code for quashment of the proceedings of the case with-out waiting for framing of charge or invoking the provisions of section 241 A of the Code for discharge. The High Court Division erred in law discharging the rule without considering the fact of the case as disclosed in the FIR and the Charge Sheet. Since no offence has been disclosed from the facts narrated in the FIR and the charge sheet, the continuation of the proceeding would amount to an abuse of the process of the Court. Therefore, we are of the view that in order to prevent the abuse of the process of the court the High Court Division should have quashed the proceeding of the case pending in the court of Magistrate, First Class, Narayangonj (South).</u>

In the facts and circumstances of the case, we are constrained to observe that the adverse remarks and observations based on surmises and conjectures are extraneous, unjust, unwarranted and unsubstantiated which case aspersions upon the conduct and professional integrity of the Advocate -Petitioners.

<u>51. It will well established that when the Appellate Court is hearing an appeal, it is very mush within the power and duty of the learned Judges to comment upon the performance and proceeding s of the trial court if these were contrary to any provision of law or had the effect of impropriety. The adverse remarks and observations or criticism offered in a case would fall within the requirements of the dispensations of the justice if the model of trial adopted by the trial Judge or the conduct of the learned Advocates in the trial court is not proper or in violation of the Cannons of the Professional Conduct and Etiquette. While making observations on the judgment of he Appellate Bench who made adverse criticism on the mode of trial adopted by the trial court, the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Syed Ali Nawas Gardezi v. Lt Col Muhammad Yusuf reported in 15 DLR (SC) 9 observed as under; "For, in all circumstances, the criticism offered would of necessity fall within the requirements of the dispensation of justice. One of the requirements is that the Judge offering the criticism upon the work of an equal, should bethink himself, more than once, of the possibility that he might himself be mistaken. In other words, he would devote more than ordinary care to the ascertainment of the facts on which his censure is to be founded. He would need to satisfy himself that the blame he lays upon his brother and the terms in which he expresses it, are both necessary for the doing of justice in the matter before him or in rarer case, for the advancement of justice generally. It is imperative that the criticism offered should not only be well-informed but also that it should be well-intentioned in a strictly judicial sense." In this case the Supreme Court of Pakistan made a caution that these are necessary conditions of any-thing said by way of admonition in a solemn judicial pronouncement "But where it is said about a judge of a superior Court if these conditions are not satisfied the mischief which might follow is of incalculable proportions, for judgment of a Court of Record" is a document of a public character, and is preserved in perpetuity. Such document of a public character, and is preserved in perpetuity. Such criticism directly diminishes the capacity of the Judge who criticized to do justice in matters coming before him. Equally, it affects the standing of the Court of which he is an integral part. For nothing is better calculated to destroy the image and the ends of justice as it has been built up in the course of many centuries than that the Judges of the Superior Courts at the apex should engage in lowering one or more of their number as instrument for the dispensation of justice in the estimation and in full view of the public. We take judicial notice of the fact that the judgment of the Full Bench, a lengthy document, appeared in a number of daily newspapers on the day after its pronouncement, including the passages to which exception has been taken. It is difficult to overstate the potentiality possessed by these passages to produce an adverse effect upon the dignity, the prestige and the integrity of the superior Courts. We are conscious that in certain circumstances, it might be necessary to take the risk of such damage, for the removal of an evil. And correspondingly, when the evil is found, not in the Judge who is criticised, but in the criticism itself, there is a call which we cannot ignore to exercise the high duty, however hard it might be, to excise the blemish, in the way of fairness to the Judge and for the restoration of true dignity to the proceedings of the Appellate bench . It is in that spirit, and bearing fully in mind the duty of proper respect to the learned Judges of that Bench that we have felt impelled to make the observations which follow."</u>

<u>52. In the case of M.A. Wahab v. State 10 BLD (AD) 50 the appellate Division while considering the criticism of a Division Bench about the order passed by a Vacation Bench observed : "At the most, it may be said, that it was indiscreet on the part of the learned Vacation Judge to have granted bail in the facts of the case, but we certainly do not approve of the manner and language in which the learned Judges have chosen to express themselves against a brother Judge of the same Court. It seems that the norms and forms of judicial decorum in the highest court even are not being properly observed and this has caused concern to us. It does not seem to have occurred to the learned Judges that the innuendoes against the petitioners are not only likely to be viewed as tendentious against a particular Judge, but they are apt to bring the Court itself into disrepute to which they themselves belong. We must express our extreme disrepute to which they themselves belong. We must express our extreme disapproval over the lack of restraint and sobriety which marks the offending paragraph."</u>

<u>53. In the foregoing paragraphs the Apex Courts of the Sub-Continent expressed their disapproval over the lack of restraint or sobriety of the Appellate Court while making observations in passing judgment about the mode of trial in the trial court. The same observations in the name of caution is very mush applicable in the case of Advocates who are discharging their professional duties before the court. The learned Members of the Bar are Officers of the Court to which they owe a duty to represent the case correctly. While speaking about the standing of the members of the Bar before the court the Appellate Division in the case of Esrarul Haq Chowdhury -vs- MD. Amir Hossain and another, 66 DLR (AD) observed: In most jurisdictions, the members of the legal profession are conferred the status of privileged members of the community and occupies an exclusive domain with the privilege of pleading and acting on behalf of suitors being restricted only to enrolled Advocates and Attorneys. The role of Advocate as Officers of the Court is to assist the Court in the administration of justice. Advocates collect materials relating to a case and thereby assist the Court in arriving at a correct judgment. Furthermore, being a responsible officer of the Court and an important adjunct of the administration of justice, the Advocate also owes a duty to the Court as well as the opposite side. Advocates, as members of the Bar and officers of the Court, have the responsibility of "keeping the stream of justice pure and unsullied "so also to enable it to administer justice fairly and to the satisfaction of al concerned. The primary duty of the Advocate is to inform the Court as to the law and facts of the case and to aid the Court to do justice by arriving at correct conclusion. Since the court acts on the basis of what is presented by the Advocates, the Advocates are under the obligation to be absolutely fair to the Court. All statements should be accurate, and the Advocate is under a sacrosanct obligation to ensure that he does not, through any act or omission lead to the possibility of misrepresentation, or mislead the Court or obfuscate the case in any manner. What is imperative to be borne in mind is that the legal profession cannot be considered like any other profession, or trade or business. It is a noble profession, which is intended to serve the cause of "justice". There is a difference between the legal profession and other professions because of the fact that advocates do affects not only an individual but the administration of justice which is the foundation of the civilized society when there is a conflict between the most specific instructions of his client and his duty to the Court, the latter takes precedence. This is a dictate not from a code of law, but a higher code of honor which, if disregarded, offends not only the rules of the profession, but strikes at the heart of the confidence of the public in the judicial system itself. If people lose confidence in the legal profession for the deviant behaviour of some of its members, it is not only the profession which will suffer but also the administration of justice as a whole. It is well established that an Advocate is not only a professional but he is an officer of the Court and his obligations as an officer of the Court are paramount. The Supreme Court of India in the case of Bar Council of Maharashtra -vs-MV Dabholkar etc. AIR 1976 SC 242 observed that an Advocate being an Officer of the Court as a public servant plays a key role in the developmental and dispute processing activities and above all in the building up of a just society and constitutional order". An Advocate being a member of the society worthy of confidence of the community in him is required to act a vehicle of social justice. If an advocate of the court commits any mistake intentionally or mislead the court to get undue advantage a duty is cast upon the court to make comment or critism on the conduct of the learned Advocate who acted in contravention of law because the criticism made would fall within the requirements of the dispensation of justice.</u>

54. But in the instant case in reality the allegation made by the learned judges in the judgment that there was suppression of facts in the quashment petition has no basis inasmuch as the accused petitioners in paragraph 7, 8, 9 and 10 of the quashment petition clearly disclosed on 02.07.2006 that the entire matter starting from granting of anticipatory bail upto issuance of warrants of arrest and their difficulty was mentioned elaborately. Moreover, certified copy of the order dated 02-07-2006 was annexed as annexure B-1 to the Supplementary Affidavit by the informant in the Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.9954 of 2006 wherefrom the learned Judges could have easily perused the contents of the same. It is unfortunate that the learned Judges completely ignored what the accused petitioners disclosed in the quashment petition before obtaining Rule and the order of Ad-interim bail. We have noticed that the Advocate-Petitioners in their Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal No.304 of 2007 clearly stated that there is no doubt as to the genuineness of the initials given by the Affidavit Commissioner inasmuch as the Advocate categorically asserted that whatever corrections were made as regards description of the accused petitioners in the cause title and amendment of the prayer portion of the petition for quashment inserting by pen "enlarge the petitioners on ad-interim bail" were duly initialed by the Affidavit Commissioner, Mr. Mahbubey Alam, the learned Attorney General found it difficult to oppose the prayer of the Advocate - petitioners for expungement of the offending remarks and observations made by the learned Judges. The circumstances for which the accused petitioners could not appear before the Court of Magistrate, First Class, Narayangonj have been clearly narrated in paragraph 7, 8, 9 and 10 of the quashment petition. We regret that we cannot endorse the views of the learned Judges about the conduct and etiquette of the Advocate -petitioners. Having considered the submissions advanced on behalf of the Advocate petitioners and perused the quashment petition and other materials on record we have come to the conclusion that without considering the facts narrated in the quashment petition and other materials on record the learned Judges misconstrued the facts and thereby misdirected themselves in making adverse remarks and observations. In view of the above discussion and findings we have no hesitation to opine that the basis of the learned Judges to make adverse remarks and observations was extremely insubstantial and hypothetical to some extent. The remarks and observations have the adverse effect upon the dignity, the prestige and the integrity of the Apex Court of which the Advocate -petitioners are officers. The carelessness displaced by the learned Judges while dealing with such a sensitive issue concerning the professional honesty and integrity of the two learned Members of the Bar, one of whom is a Senior Advocate of this Court and a former President of the Supreme Court Bar Association and the other member is a promising Advocate of the Bar. It is well established that one of the necessary conditions for validity of censure of the work of the learned Members of the Bar of the Apex Court of the country should be well -informed and well-intentioned in the judicial sense.

55. To make adverse remarks and observations against the learned Advocates alleging suppression of material facts as stated above would be tentamount to blaming them for no fault of their own.

<u>56. The proceeding of the case was very unusual in the sense that the accused petitioners of the quashment petition who had been earlier granted anticipatory bail in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No 6238 of 2006 surrendered before the Court of Magistrate, First class, Narayangonj who granted bail on submission of bail bond as per order of the High Court Division Fixing the next date on 02.07.2006 for appearance. But because of "oborodh" (siege) observed by the opposition political parties at that time and the unusual prevailed in the Dhaka City the accused petitioners having faced such situation filed an application for extension of bail stating that on the date fixed for appearance before the Magistrate they could not appear and that their bail was cancelled by the Magistrate and that for this special reason they having appeared before the High Court Division sought quashment of the proceedings and a prayer for bail was made therein and a prayer for bail was made therein. From the above discussion it is abundantly clear that in the quashment petition all relevant facts were disclosed and there was no suppression of facts. This Division consistently held that when a warrant of arrest is issued against an accused person, he should at the earliest opportunity, surrender before the competent Court and make necessary prayer for relief, but without surrendering before the competent Court he should not be present directly before the High Court Division for seeking relief.</u>

57. We have already perused that the learned Judges after concluding the judgment, discharging the Rule and ordering for sending down lower courts records proceeded to add another eleven pages entirely on the conduct of the Advocate -Petitioners making some unwarranted, uncalled for, unjust and extraneous remarks and observations. This part of the judgment is extraneous to the subject matter of the Rule which demonstrates the bias of the learned Judges against the Advocate Petitioners. Such observations touching the honesty, integrity and conduct of the Advocate -petitioners as professional Lawyers were based upon a wrongful finding that the order of Rule, stay of proceedings and ad interim bail was obtained by suppressing the fact that warrants of arrest had been issued against the accused, whereas in reality the fact of the said issuance of warrants of arrest including the circumstances leading to their filing of the application for extension of bail was expressly narrated in the petition for quashment. From our scrutiny, we are of the view that the remarks and observations being extremely insubstantial and to some extent hypothetical are extraneous to the merit of the Case based upon findings and premises which are contrary to the records of the case and not relevant to the disposal of the rule in dispensing justice.

58. The fact of the adverse remarks and observation is nothing but a supplement to the main judgment which being extraneous tot the merit of the case was not necessary for dispensing justice in the case. In view of the foregoing discussions and findings we are convinced to hold that the adverse remarks and observations, not being well-informed and well-intentioned, constitute aspersion and blemish upon the professional conduct and etiquette of the Advocate -Petitioners. For the aforesaid reasons, the adverse remarks and observations made in paragraphs 3, 6, 8, 9, 10 and 11 of the Judgment of the High Court Division being extraneous and without any basis is not well -informed and well intentioned and these paragraphs contain matter which was not necessary to dispense justice in disposing of Rule in the case or generally and therefore, the offending remarks and observations should be expunged in the interest of justice. Paragraphs 12 to 16 contain leading decisions of the Sub-Continent which have no relevance with the facts and circumstances of the instant case and there-fore these are liable to be expunged. Adverse remarks and observations made in paragraph 17 being extraneous to the facts of the case is liable to be expunged. Paragraphs 24 to 37 are Supplementary to the judgment passed by the High Court Division which is not necessary for dispensing justice in disposing of the Rule. Paragraph 24 contains adverse remarks against the Advocate-petitioners without any basis, therefore, this paragraph is liable to be expunged Paragraphs 25 to 34 contain discussion on leading decisions of the Apex Courts of the subcontinent which are not at all relevant of disposal of the Rule and accordingly these are liable to be expunged. Paragraphs 35 to 37 devoted to adverse remarks and observations against the Advocate petitioners without any basis which not being fair, well-informed and well-intentioned nor they intended to serve the ends of justice and as much these are liable to be expunged.

<u>59. It is well established that the learned Judges of the court in which a case /appeal in disposed of have the power and duty to comment or make remark and observation on the conduct of the learned Advocate who has represented his clients before the Court if his conduct is unfair or in violation of Cannons of Professional Conduct and Etiquette. The criticism in respect of conduct of the learned Advocate depends on the gravity of the irregularity committed by the learned Advocate while discharging his duty as an Officer of the Court. If the conduct of the learned Advocate is unfair or in violation of Cannons of Professional Conduct and Etiquette the purpose of criticism or adverse remarks and observation made against the learned Advocate would be within the requirements of dispensation of justice. The learned Judges should remember that the criticism or adverse remarks and observation would be necessary for dispensation of justice in the matter before them or for advancement of justice generally. The learned Judges should be very cautious when making criticism or adverse remark and observation against the learned Advocate who has appeared before them because it may have the adverse effect upon the dignity and the integrity of the superior courts. When a criticism or remark and observation is made against an Advocate without any basis, a high duty is cast upon appellate court to expunge the wrong criticism or adverse remarks and observation in the way of fairness to the Advocate who is criticized without having any opportunity to explain the matters held against him which is ill founded and unnecessary for determination of the matter before the court. A wrong criticism would have the effect of making his professional honesty and integrity questionable and undermining his position as an Officer of the Court in the Society. At the same time it has to be noted that no comment on mistaken view would be made about the mode of trial adopted by the learned Judge of the trial court or the manner in which learned Judge of the lower Appellate Court has conducted the proceedings of the court which would have effect of destroying the image and the edifice of justice. The Judges of the Appellate Court should remember that in certain circumstances it is imperative to comment or make adverse remark on the judgment where the criticism or remark and observation made by the learned Judge of the trial court or the lower Appellate Court is faulty or in contravention of law or had the effect of unfairness or impropriety. In the premises, the Appellate Court has to exercise the high duty, however harsh it may be, to expunge the offending remark or criticism about a Judge or an Advocate in the way of bringing fairness to the learned Judge or the Advocate and for restoration of true dignity to the proceedings of the Court who made the remark or criticism without any basis. The Judges of the Appellate Court have to bear in mind that the power to make fair comment, on the mode of trial or any irregularity committed by the learned Judge of the trial court or by the learned Advocate who appears before the Court in discharging his professional duty, should be necessary to remove any fault which is in the criticism or remarks not in the Judge or the Advocate who is criticized in the way of fairness to him and for restoration of true dignity to the proceeding of the appellate court.</u>

60. From the above discussion and observations we find merit in the Criminal Appeal No.35 of 2010 and accordingly, the appeal in allowed. The impugned judgment and order dated 04-07-2007 discharging the Rule in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.11080 of 2006 is set aside and consequently, Fatullah P.S. Case No. 125 dated 27.04.2006 under sections 406/420/506 of the Penal Code pending in the Court of Magistrate, First Class, Narayangonj (South) so far as it relates to the appellant is quashed.

61. The adverse remarks and observations in paragraphs 3, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 17, 24, 25, 35, 36 and 37 of the impugned judgment and order are expunged Paragraphs 12-16 and 25-33, 34 of the impugned judgment and other being discussions on leading decisions of the Apex Court of the country which have no relevance with the facts and circumstances of the instant case are also expunged. The Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal No.304 of 2007 is disposed of with observations and expunctions as stated above.
